title: The beautiful blue-haired Girl has the puppet brought in: she puts him to bed and calls three doctors to find out whether he is alive or dead.
paragraphs: While poor Pinocchio, whom the murderers had hanged from a branch of the Great Oak, now seemed more dead than alive, the beautiful blue-haired Girl appeared at the window again, and taking pity on the unhappy creature who, hanging by his neck, was dancing in the blasts of the north wind, she clapped her hands three times, making three little sounds.
At this signal there was a great beating of wings rushing through the air, and a large Falcon landed on the windowsill.

“What are your orders, my kind Fairy?” said the Falcon, lowering his beak in a bow; for you should know that the blue-haired Girl was, after all, none other than a very good Fairy who had lived near that wood for more than a thousand years.
“Do you see that puppet hanging from a branch of the Great Oak?”
“I see him.”
“Well then: fly there at once; use your very strong beak to break the knot that holds him in the air, and lay him gently on the grass at the foot of the Oak.”
The Falcon flew away, and two minutes later he returned, saying:
“What you ordered is done.”
“And how did you find him? Alive or dead?”
“He looked dead, but he cannot be quite dead yet, because as soon as I loosened the rope loop around his throat, he gave a sigh and stammered quietly, ‘Now I feel better!’”
Then the Fairy clapped her hands twice, making two little sounds, and a magnificent Poodle appeared, walking upright on his hind legs exactly like a man.

The Poodle was dressed in a coachman’s finest uniform. On his head he wore a little three-cornered hat trimmed with gold, a blond wig with curls falling down his neck, a chocolate-coloured coat with diamond buttons and two large pockets for the bones his mistress gave him at dinner, short trousers of deep red velvet, silk stockings, low-cut shoes, and behind him something like an umbrella cover, made entirely of blue satin, to put his tail inside when it began to rain.

“Come on, good boy, Medoro!” the Fairy said to the Poodle. “Have the finest carriage in my stable harnessed at once, and take the road to the wood. When you reach the Great Oak, you will find a poor half-dead puppet lying on the grass. Pick him up gently, lay him flat on the carriage cushions and bring him here to me. Do you understand?”
To show that he understood, the Poodle wagged the blue satin cover behind him three or four times, and set off like a racehorse.

A little later, a beautiful little sky-coloured carriage came out of the stable, padded all over with canary feathers and lined inside with whipped cream and custard with sponge biscuits. The little carriage was pulled by a hundred pairs of white mice, and the Poodle, sitting on the driver’s seat, cracked his whip right and left, like a driver afraid he was running late.

Less than a quarter of an hour had passed when the little carriage returned, and the Fairy, who was waiting at the door, took the poor puppet in her arms and carried him into a little room with mother-of-pearl walls, then sent at once for the most famous doctors in the neighbourhood.
And the doctors arrived at once, one after another: that is, a Raven, a Little Owl and a Talking Cricket.

“I would like you gentlemen to tell me,” said the Fairy, speaking to the three doctors gathered around Pinocchio’s bed, “I would like you gentlemen to tell me whether this unfortunate puppet is alive or dead!”
At this invitation, the Raven stepped forward first and felt Pinocchio’s pulse; then he felt his nose, then his little toes: and after feeling very carefully, he spoke these solemn words:
“In my opinion, the puppet is quite dead: but if, unfortunately, he were not dead, that would be a sure sign that he is still alive!”

“I am sorry,” said the Little Owl, “to have to disagree with the Raven, my famous friend and fellow doctor; in my opinion, on the contrary, the puppet is still alive; but if, unfortunately, he were not alive, that would be a sign that he is truly dead.”
“And have you nothing to say?” the Fairy asked the Talking Cricket.
“I say that when a careful doctor does not know what he is talking about, the best thing he can do is keep quiet. Besides, that puppet’s face is not new to me: I have known him for a long time!”
Pinocchio, who until then had stayed as still as a real piece of wood, gave a sudden shudder that shook the whole bed.
“That puppet,” the Talking Cricket went on, “is a first-class rascal…”
Pinocchio opened his eyes and closed them again at once.
“He is a naughty boy, a lazy fellow, a wanderer…”
Pinocchio hid his face under the sheets.
“That puppet is a disobedient son who will make his poor father die of a broken heart!”

At this point, a muffled sound of crying and sobbing could be heard in the room. Imagine everyone’s surprise when, lifting the sheets a little, they discovered that the one crying and sobbing was Pinocchio.
“When a dead person cries, it is a sign that he is getting better,” said the Raven solemnly.
“I am sorry to disagree with my famous friend and fellow doctor,” added the Little Owl, “but in my opinion, when a dead person cries, it is a sign that he is sorry to die.”
